title: Proposition One: Reproductive Freedom & Privacy Act

context.text: Citizen initiative. The Secretary of State's Initiatives & Amendments page lists it as qualified, saying it has met the statutory requirements to appear on the November 3, 2026 ballot. The pamphlet's arguments for were provided by Idahoans United for Women & Families, and arguments against by the Idaho Family Policy Center, Idaho Chooses Life, Right to Life Idaho, Too Extreme for Idaho, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise. If approved, the act takes effect January 1, 2027.

question.text: Short Ballot Title: Measure creating right to abortion before fetus viability, and post-viability to protect health; right to privacy; healthcare provider liability protections. Long Ballot Title: The measure seeks to change Idaho’s laws by introducing a right to reproductive freedom and privacy including a right to abortion up to the point of the fetus’s ability to survive outside the womb. After fetal viability, there would be no general right to abortion except in cases of “medical emergency.” The “medical emergency” exception would expand Idaho’s current life exception and allow abortions when pregnant women face complicating physical conditions that threaten their life or health, “including serious impairment to a bodily function” or “serious dysfunction of any bodily organ or part.” The proposed measure codifies a right to make reproductive decisions, including contraception, fertility treatment, and prenatal and postpartum care. This includes a “right of privacy” in making these decisions. The measure seeks to prevent the state from enforcing certain abortion laws protecting the life of the unborn child. It would also impose a requirement that any restrictions on reproductive decisions, including abortion prior to fetus viability, must be “narrowly tailored to improve or maintain the health of the person seeking reproductive health care.” The measure would also prevent the state from penalizing patients, healthcare providers, or anyone who assists in exercising the proposed right.

summary.text: Per the official long ballot title, the measure would create a statutory right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including a right to abortion up to fetal viability and, after viability, only in cases of “medical emergency” (an exception that is broader than Idaho's current life exception), codify a right to make reproductive decisions including contraception, fertility treatment, and prenatal and postpartum care, require that restrictions be “narrowly tailored to improve or maintain the health of the person seeking reproductive health care,” and prevent the state from penalizing patients, providers, or others who assist in exercising the right. Fiscal impact (Idaho Division of Financial Management): the State estimates state expenditures would increase between $3,100 and $7,800 annually, less than 0.001% of the state share of Idaho's Medicaid budget, derived from the cost of treating chemical-abortion complications for women enrolled in Medicaid; DFM says it “cannot in good faith conclude that the proposed initiative will have no fiscal impact on state expenditures.”

measure.yesMeans: A YES vote would support creating a right to abortion before fetal viability—defined as a fetus’ ability to survive without extraordinary medical measures—and after fetal viability in cases of medical emergency; providing protections against professional discipline and civil and criminal liability for healthcare providers; and codifying a statutory reproductive right to freedom and privacy.
measure.noMeans: A NO vote would support making no change to Idaho’s current law, which preserves the life of preborn children by prohibiting abortion, except when necessary to prevent the death of the pregnant woman, and during the first trimester in documented cases of rape or incest reported to law enforcement.

argumentsFor.text: Argument for, provided by Idahoans United for Women & Families (bullets in the pamphlet): “Voting YES would restore the standard Idaho operated under for nearly 50 years, with health and life exceptions to the abortion ban, including cases of fatal fetal diagnosis.” and “Voting YES would protect doctors and nurses from criminal prosecution for providing standard medical care, at a time when Idaho is already losing OB-GYNs, family doctors, and emergency physicians.”

Argument for, provided by Idahoans United for Women & Families (bullets in the pamphlet): “Voting YES does NOT create public funding for abortion, nor does it force any provider to violate their conscience.” and “Voting YES does NOT change Idaho’s current parental consent laws: all healthcare for minors would still require the permission of a parent or guardian.”

Rebuttal to the arguments against, provided by Idahoans United for Women & Families: “Abortion remains illegal after viability under Proposition One, except when a doctor determines it is medically necessary to protect the woman’s life or health.”

argumentsAgainst.text: Argument against, provided by the Idaho Family Policy Center, Idaho Chooses Life, Right to Life Idaho, Too Extreme for Idaho, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise: “Prop 1 claims to allow abortions only to the point of ‘viability’ but throws out the longstanding definition of that term. Idaho law has always defined ‘fetal viability’ as the point at which a baby could ‘potentially live outside the mother’s womb, albeit with artificial aid.’ But Prop 1 redefines viability as the point when a baby has a ‘significant likelihood of sustained survival without extraordinary medical measures.’”

Argument against (same authors): “Prop 1 also eliminates the longstanding safety requirement that only doctors can perform abortions. It replaces ‘physician’ with the vague term ‘health care provider,’ which it defines as any ‘licensed person or entity that provides health care or medical treatment.’”

Argument against (same authors): “But perhaps the most shocking of all? Prop 1 authorizes ‘health care providers’ to perform abortions on teenage girls behind the backs of their parents, overturning parental consent requirements. That’s because Prop 1 creates a right to abortion for ‘every person’ regardless of age, making abortion the only procedure that could be performed on a child without parental involvement.”

currentLaw.text: Idaho's existing laws ban nearly all abortions, with exceptions to prevent the death of the pregnant woman and, in the first trimester, in cases of rape or incest reported to law enforcement; providers face felony penalties, licensing penalties and civil suits (Idaho Capital Sun). The Secretary of State's voter pamphlet describes current law the same way in its "What your vote will do" text, and its long ballot title says the measure's "medical emergency" exception would expand Idaho's current life exception.

fiscalImpact.text: The Idaho Division of Financial Management estimates state expenditures would increase by $3,100 to $7,800 a year, less than 0.001 percent of the state share of the Medicaid budget, based on assumed Medicaid-covered complications from chemical abortions (about 300 Medicaid recipients, with complications for 6 to 15 of them at an average state cost of about $531). It says it "cannot in good faith conclude that the proposed initiative will have no fiscal impact on state expenditures." The sponsors' funding source statement says the act creates no new financial obligation and has no effect on taxes.

supporters.text: Idahoans United for Women & Families (sponsor; its PAC is chaired by Meridian OB-GYN Becky Uranga)

opponents.text: Too Extreme for Idaho (PAC chaired by Katherine Heffner)

campaignFinance.text: As of Sept. 29, 2026, per the Idaho Secretary of State campaign finance database as analyzed by the Idaho Capital Sun: the Idahoans United for Women and Families PAC (supporting) had raised about $4.9 million from more than 3,000 donors and spent more than $1.1 million, with about $3.2 million of its contributions from Idaho and $1.7 million from out of state; the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC (opposing) had raised about $2.5 million from 83 donors and spent nearly $169,000, nearly all from Idaho donors. The Sun noted that spending on both sides may be undercounted because of inconsistent measure names in the state database.

sources.title: 2026 Idaho General Election: ballot measures and Idaho Voter Pamphlet text
Supporters and opponents of Idaho's abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions

researchNotes: Ballot list confirmed against the Secretary of State's VoteIdaho.gov General Election page, which lists exactly four statewide items (HJR 4, HJR 6, Proposition One, and the State Gun advisory question). Question text combines the short and long ballot titles as published on VoteIdaho.gov. The official fiscal impact statement was written by the Division of Financial Management and covers only the Medicaid cost estimate described. The arguments for and against are partisan committee statements printed in the pamphlet; the two sides disagree on parental-consent, physician and viability-definition effects, and the proponents' rebuttal points readers to the official ballot summary. Wording from both sides' pamphlet statements is quoted as published, including characterizations of the other side. Enrichment: the voter pamphlet (read from raw PDF text) was used for the fiscal figures and sponsor/opponent names; finance totals are the Idaho Capital Sun's reading of Secretary of State filings as of Sept. 29, not the filings themselves. Two quotations in the arguments were repaired to match the pamphlet's wording exactly (the pamphlet prints them as bullets).
